import plotly.graph_objects as go
from twinfault_site import *

totals = sql("""
    select sum(transfers) as transfers, min(date) as first_day, max(date) as last_day,
           count(distinct date) as days, count(distinct month) as months
    from fct_daily_payments
""").iloc[0]
pipe = sql("""
    select sum(blocks) as blocks, sum(missing_blocks) + sum(duplicate_blocks) as gaps
    from fct_daily_pipeline
""").iloc[0]
tests = dbt_test_count()
span = f"{totals.first_day:%b %Y} to {totals.last_day:%b %Y}"
months = int(totals.months)
blocks_note = "Ethereum blocks, none missing or duplicated" if pipe.gaps == 0 else "Ethereum blocks checked for gaps"
tests_value = str(tests) if tests else "dbt"
tests_note = "dbt tests passed by every month" if tests else "tests on every month"
```

# Is it the business, or the pipeline?

[When a payments metric suddenly moves, the first question is whether customers changed or the data did. A late file or a duplicated load can look exactly like a real drop. **twinfault** finds every unusual day in every USDT, USDC and PYUSD transfer on Ethereum since January 2024, checks the pipeline first, and decides with evidence which it was.]{.lead}

monthly = sql("""
    select month, token, sum(transfers) as transfers
    from fct_daily_payments group by all order by month
""")
fig = go.Figure()
for token in TOKENS:
    d = monthly[monthly.token == token]
    fig.add_bar(x=d.month, y=d.transfers, name=token, marker_color=TOKEN_COLORS[token],
                hovertemplate="%{y:.3s}")
fig.update_layout(barmode="stack", bargap=0.18)
fig.update_yaxes(tickformat="~s")
show(fig, height=340)
```

## The look-alike pairs

Every metric move has two possible explanations that look the same on a dashboard: a pipeline fault, or a real change in behaviour. The metric alone cannot separate them; the rows can. The table lists the pairs and the evidence that separates them. Most of these checks run automatically on [every unusual day](watch.html).

::: {.twins .tf-scroll}
| Pipeline fault | Business twin | Same headline effect | Evidence that separates them |
|---|---|---|---|
| A day's partition not loaded | Real network slowdown | Volume drops | Gaps in block numbers vs continuous blocks with fewer transfers |
| Same data loaded twice | Genuine surge | Volume jumps | Repeated transaction hashes vs unique ones |
| Late-arriving data | Real slowdown that day | Yesterday looks low | Load time lags block time, then backfills |
| Decimals bug, values off by a power of 10 | Real surge in large transfers | Average value jumps | Exact 10× factor vs a shifted distribution |
| Classification rule changed | Real mix shift | Segment shares move | Rule version changed while raw data did not |
| Timezone bug | Real change in hourly pattern | Hourly profile shifts | Constant whole-hour offset |
| Filter drops failed transactions | Real fall in failures | Failure rate falls | Raw and modelled counts disagree |
:::

Blockchain data suits this unusually well: block numbers are sequential and transaction hashes are unique, so completeness and duplicates can be checked from the data itself.

```{python}
#| output: asis
known = value_outliers().dropna(subset=["reason"])
if not known.empty:
    k = known.iloc[0]
    print(f"""<div class="real-twin"><p><b>A real twin, found in this data.</b>
On {k.date:%d %B %Y}, {k.token} value moved was {compact(k.volume, "$")}, about
{compact(k.times_usual)} times its median day. On a dashboard that looks exactly like a decimals bug.
It wasn't one. {k.reason} (<a href="{k.source}" target="_blank">source</a>). The data was right,
and the <a href="investigations.html#pyusd-mint">investigation</a> shows it from the data itself.
Telling cases like this apart, before anyone explains them, is what twinfault tests.</p></div>""")
```

## How it is built

```{python}
#| output: asis
steps = [
    ("Source", "AWS Public Blockchain Data", "Ethereum as Parquet on S3"),
    ("Extract", "DuckDB on GitHub Actions", "a month per job, seven checks"),
    ("Store", "Hugging Face dataset", "one folder per day, free and public"),
    ("Model", "dbt on DuckDB", f"daily marts, {tests or 'all'} tests a month"),
    ("Publish", "Quarto on GitHub Pages", "this site, rebuilt from the marts"),
]
cells = "".join(
    f'<div class="step"><div class="step-kicker">{k}</div><div class="step-name">{n}</div>'
    f'<div class="step-note">{d}</div></div>' for k, n, d in steps
)
print(f'<div class="flow column-page">{cells}</div>')
```

- **Extract:** DuckDB reads the AWS public Parquet files straight from S3 on free GitHub runners, a month per job and four months at a time. Each month must pass seven checks before upload.
- **Model:** dbt on DuckDB builds staging tables and three daily marts for each month. A month is published only if every test passes, including a reconciliation that the daily cube adds up to the raw transfers.
- **Publish:** Quarto rebuilds this site from the marts and GitHub Pages hosts it. Every number on it is computed from the published data at build time. There is no server and no subscription.
